title: control-plane-boundary-charter-and-owner-roster
content:
Purpose
This note sketches a compact charter for control-plane boundaries and a pragmatic owner roster mapped to observable responsibilities. Goal is to reduce ambiguity during region failover, deployments, and team handoffs. Treat this as a working ledger — iterative, intentionally opinionated.

Context & motivation
- We have three logical surfaces that often get blurred in incident and rollout time: ingress (API gateway + edge proxies), orchestration/control-plane (scheduling, routing policy decisions, rollout state), and runtime adapters (region/hardware-specific agents that talk to serving runtime).
- Confusion in past incidents: who owns circuit-breaking when a region reports high GPU queue depth? API gateway implemented a quick 429; platform teams expected the orchestrator to re-route. The short answer: both have a role, but the ownership boundaries were not explicit.

High-level boundary principles
1) Keep decision responsibility close to the signal source.
   - If an event originates at the runtime (e.g., memory pressure, kernel OOM, adapter heartbeat loss), runtime adapters signal and are primarily responsible for local mitigation (graceful reject, scaledown hooks).
2) Keep routing policy enforcement at the orchestrator layer, not at edge.
   - The orchestrator is the source-of-truth for consistent routing policies, multi-region preferences, and model-version constraints. API gateway enforces fast-path protections (rate limits, per-tenant quotas) but defers global routing choices to orchestrator.
3) API gateway ≠ orchestration.
   - API gateway: low-latency ingress, auth, request shaping, token-level quota enforcement, basic retries.
   - Orchestrator(control-plane): policy engine, rollout state, global routing decisions, fallback chains, canary/A-B splits, and long-lived reconciliation.
4) Runtime adapters act as guardians of physical resources.
   - They expose health streams, capacity, and feature capabilities (quantization support, preferred kernel). Adapters own local remediation and machine-level maintenance procedures.

Concrete ownership roster (proposal)
- API Gateway / Edge Proxy: eng-platform-networking (owner)
  - Responsibilities: ingress auth, TLS termination, global rate limits, first-chance request shaping, telemetry emission for request latency and error rates, short-circuit responses during overload.
  - SLOs: 99.9% request accept path < 8ms (happy path), < 500ms for proxying.

- Control Plane / Orchestrator: eng-platform-engineering (owner)
  - Responsibilities: routing policy decision engine, region preferences, canary rollouts, model-version tagging, reconciliation loops, routing fallback matrix, persisted routing state, policy auditing.
  - SLOs: Decision propagation < 15s for critical policy changes; consistency windows clearly documented per-policy.

- Runtime Adapters (region/node-level agents): eng-serving-runtime + infra-k8s-team (shared)
  - Responsibilities: local resource monitoring, capacity reporting, local circuit-breakers, graceful drain flows, runtime-level kernel selection flags, region-local cache invalidation hooks.
  - SLOs: Health heartbeat < 10s, capacity updates within 30s of major topology changes.

Inter-surface contracts (APIs & messages)
- Adapter -> Orchestrator: periodic capacity delta + immediate alerts on state change (json payload with: adapter_id, region, gpu_types, free_slots, max_seq_len_supported, current_queue_depth, timestamp).
- Orchestrator -> Adapter: routing directives (push: list of route rules with ids, TTL, model variants allowed), maintenance commands (drain, emergency-disable).
- API Gateway -> Orchestrator: flow-probe telemetry and per-tenant throttling events. Gateway requests orchestration decisions via a fast decision cache; on cache miss, orchestrator provides authoritative routing.

Routing policy decomposition (examples)
- Latency-first route: prefer local region runtime adapters with spare capacity and matching kernel features; fallback to cross-region when expected added RTT <= 150ms and cost delta < configured threshold.
- Cost-first route: prefer lower-cost instance pool (quantized variant) unless user has pinned model version or quality criteria unmet.
- Geo-compliance route: force VPC/private-only variants if tenant requires isolation; orchestrator enforces policy and returns 403 if no compliant adapter is available.

Multi-region failover sequence (recommended playbook)
1) Adapter signals degraded state (heartbeats missing / high queue depth). Adapter does local short-circuit to protect node.
2) Orchestrator marks adapter as degraded and immediately recalculates routing. Pushes routing delta to gateway cache and to other adapters as needed.
3) Gateway applies soft-redirects (503 vs 429 depending on tenant preferences) until orchestrator decision propagates.
4) If orchestrator cannot find acceptable capacity within failover budget, apply automatic downgrade policy (model quantization or reduced max_seq_len) or engage reserved capacity (dedicated pools) per tenant commit.
5) Postmortem: orchestrator emits a single canonical incident note with timeline + owners.

Ownership decision log (short entries)
- When a route-level policy has global impact (e.g., turning on cross-region fallbacks), eng-platform-engineering and eng-platform-networking must approve.
- Runtime adapters may emergency-disable themselves for safety; such actions must create a high-priority ticket to eng-platform-engineering automatically.

Observability mapping (who owns which telemetry)
- Gateway: request ingress traces, auth failures, per-token cost meter.
- Orchestrator: policy decision traces, routing change events, per-route consistency metrics.
- Runtime adapter: capacity timeseries, kernel selection logs, GPU queue depth histograms.
- Ownership: each emitted metric should include an owner tag to simplify on-call routing (owner:team_name).

Operational playbooks & handoffs
- Deploying a new routing policy: create PR in platform-control-plane repo -> unit tests for decision engine + simulation (synthetic load) -> staged rollout using canary tenants -> monitor decision discrepancy metrics -> full roll. Reviewer: policy-owner in eng-platform-engineering.
- Incident triage quick script: run `pl-ctl health --region X --model Y` which queries orchestrator + adapter health + gateway probe; output includes owner hints. Add to SRE runbook.

Open questions and proposals
- Cache coherence model: should gateway keep only a short-lived cache and always consult orchestrator for first request per route? Proposal: gateway holds a bounded decision cache with TTL 10s for non-safety-critical tenants; safety-critical tenants bypass cache.
- Decision audit trail: how verbose should orchestrator's audit logs be? Proposal: keep compact (policy id + decision reason + fingerprint) for 90 days, full debug traces for 14 days.
- Cross-team SLA mapping: need explicit mapping between SLOs and oncall responsibilities for 3 tiers (edge, control-plane, runtime). Draft to be converted to table in follow-up doc.

Action items (next-week sprint)
- Aisha: prototype adapter -> orchestrator capacity delta schema and write lightweight CLI (PLT-4988).
- Mariela: add gateway cache bypass flag for safety-critical tenants (PR target: platform-networking repo).
- Liam: simulate multi-region failover scenarios for two model families and produce decision latency histogram.
- Owen: write runbook skeleton for incident handoffs across the three surfaces.

Appendix: illustrative owner roster snapshot
- eng-platform-networking: API Gateway
- eng-platform-engineering: Orchestrator / control-plane
- eng-serving-runtime: Runtime adapters implementation
- infra-k8s-team: Node maintenance and k8s operator integration
- eng-observability: central telemetry ingestion and alert routing

Notes to reviewers
This is intentionally concise. The goal is to make oncall time and rollout time decisions deterministic through clear boundaries and lightweight contracts. Please comment inline with concrete counter-proposals and add links to existing PRs or tickets.
